chunks: Inductor differential equation. The question: What is the differential equation for an inductor?
The inductor equation is v equals L di over dt . The voltage across an inductor equals its inductance times how fast the current is changing.
Turn it around and it says the current is the running total of the voltage you have applied. A constant voltage makes the current ramp up steadily.
A zero voltage makes the current hold steady.
Think of driving a car. The gas pedal is the voltage, and your speed is the current. Holding the pedal steady does not hold your speed steady.
It makes your speed rise at a steady rate. Take your foot off and you keep your speed.
The inductance is like the car's mass: a heavier car needs more push for the same change in speed. An ideal inductor has no friction, which real cars do.
Current i L enters the terminal marked +. With that choice, v L = +L di L/dt and the power vi is the power absorbed by the inductor.
Rate of change ( di over dt ): how many amps per second the current is rising or falling. Inductance (L): the constant that links voltage and the rate of change of current.
Running total (integral): the current is the sum of all the voltage applied so far, divided by L . Ramp: a straight-line rise, which is what a constant voltage gives.
Volt-second balance: in steady state, the up-ramps and down-ramps of current cancel out.
Put 10 volts across a 1 millihenries inductor. The current rises at di over dt equals V over L equals 10 over 0. 001 equals 10 000 amps/s, which is 1 amps every 100 microseconds.
Now set the voltage to 0 volts and the current stays where it is, because di over dt equals 0 . At DC an ideal inductor is just a wire. That is the whole idea.
"It's v equals L di over dt : inductor voltage equals inductance times the rate of change of current, with current into the plus terminal.
In integral form, i(t) equals i(t 0) plus 1 over L the integral of v dt , so the current is the running integral of the voltage.
A constant voltage gives a linear current ramp, constant current means zero voltage so it's a short at DC, and the current can't jump instantly without infinite voltage.
That's the basis of buck converter ripple and volt-second balance."
